ai.definition: Fusion Net-Energy Demonstrators are experimental devices designed to produce more energy from nuclear fusion than is required to operate them, marking a significant milestone in the journey towards practical fusion power plants.
ai.howItWorks: These demonstrators use high-temperature superconducting magnets to confine and sustain a hot plasma. Alternatively, they may employ lasers to compress fuel pellets. The goal is to achieve conditions where nuclear fusion reactions release more energy than was input during the process of maintaining or initiating the reaction.
ai.problemSolved: The challenge of producing net-energy from fusion has been one of the major barriers in realizing practical fusion power plants. Demonstrators address this by showing that under certain conditions, a net-positive energy output can be achieved.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing these devices involves complex engineering and materials science to create superconducting magnets capable of withstanding high temperatures and magnetic fields, as well as precise control systems for plasma confinement or laser compression.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes designing the device architecture, fabricating the superconducting magnets, assembling the core components, and integrating advanced diagnostic tools to monitor plasma behavior. Testing phases are extensive to ensure reliability and safety before net-energy operation can be demonstrated.
ai.costDrivers: High costs stem from the use of superconducting materials, precise laser systems, and complex diagnostics. Additionally, the need for ultra-high vacuum systems and extremely high temperatures contribute significantly to overall expenses.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: The outlook is promising but faces significant technical challenges that must be overcome before commercialization can occur. Continued research and development are essential to refine designs and reduce costs.
ai.regulation: Current regulatory frameworks are not yet fully equipped to handle the unique aspects of fusion energy, such as safety concerns related to high-energy plasma and radioactive materials. New regulations may need to be developed or existing ones adapted.
ai.risks: Technical risks include achieving sustained net-positive energy output, managing the complexity of superconducting systems, and ensuring long-term stability and safety of the devices. Environmental risks are minimal due to the use of non-fossil fuels, but there is a risk of radioactive waste generation from tritium breeding.
ai.profitability: Profitability at this stage is not feasible as these are primarily research tools. However, successful demonstration could lead to significant long-term economic benefits through reduced energy costs and carbon emissions.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future development will likely focus on improving the efficiency of net-energy production, reducing operational costs, and scaling up the technology for broader applications beyond demonstration purposes.

glossary.def: The difference between the energy output from a fusion device and the energy input required to maintain or initiate the reaction.
Superconducting materials capable of operating at high temperatures, used in fusion devices to confine plasma through magnetic fields.

subsystems.name: Confinement system
subsystems.role: creates the magnetic bottle or laser drive that holds or compresses the fusion fuel.

subsystems.name: Fuel and target system
subsystems.role: supplies deuterium–tritium gas or cryogenic fuel pellets.

subsystems.name: Heating and current drive
subsystems.role: brings the plasma to fusion temperature and sustains it.

subsystems.name: Vacuum vessel and first wall
subsystems.role: maintains vacuum, absorbs heat and shields components from neutrons.

subsystems.name: Diagnostics and control
subsystems.role: measures plasma conditions in real time and stabilises the discharge.

subsystems.name: Exhaust and power handling
subsystems.role: removes heat and helium ash; future plants would convert heat to electricity.

buildSteps.title: Design and simulate
buildSteps.detail: Supercomputer models choose the geometry and operating scenario that should reach net energy.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate magnets or laser optics
buildSteps.detail: For magnetic devices, superconducting coils are wound and tested; for laser devices, large crystals and precision optics are grown and polished.

buildSteps.title: Build the vacuum vessel or target chamber
buildSteps.detail: A steel torus is welded to tight tolerances, or a target chamber is assembled with ports for beams and diagnostics.

buildSteps.title: Install confinement and heating
buildSteps.detail: Magnets are placed around the vessel, or laser beams are aligned to the target chamber; neutral beams and RF antennas are added.

buildSteps.title: Add diagnostics and control
buildSteps.detail: Sensors and software are installed to measure and steer the plasma or laser shots in real time.

buildSteps.title: Commission with hydrogen
buildSteps.detail: First plasma or first laser shots are run without fusion fuel to test systems safely.

buildSteps.title: Introduce deuterium–tritium
buildSteps.detail: The machine operates with fusion fuel to measure whether energy released exceeds energy absorbed.

buildSteps.title: Capture heat (future step)
buildSteps.detail: Only a follow-on power plant would carry neutron heat to exchangers and a turbine to make electricity.

prerequisites.why: they allow stronger fields and smaller, cheaper magnetic devices, but full-scale coils for a net-energy machine are still being built.
laser fusion at the National Ignition Facility reached target gain greater than one in 2022, proving the principle.
net energy requires stable operation for long enough without instabilities that damage the machine.
tritium has been used in experiments, but breeding it from lithium at the needed scale is not yet demonstrated.
walls must survive years of fusion neutron bombardment, which no tested material can yet do in a power plant.

pathway.milestone: ITER is under construction; NIF has achieved target gain greater than one; compact high-field tokamaks such as SPARC are being built
pathway.unlocks: integrated tests of the systems needed for net energy.

pathway.milestone: first magnetic fusion device to release more energy than is absorbed by the plasma
pathway.unlocks: proof that magnetic confinement can reach net energy.

pathway.milestone: demonstration of electricity generation from fusion heat
pathway.unlocks: a complete power-plant cycle, including blankets and turbines.

pathway.milestone: commercial fusion plants with tritium breeding and reliable materials
